summary.text: 子 is a whole-graph pictograph interpreted as an infant. Its earliest supported lexical sense is “infant”; other uses, including “child” and the first earthly branch, have different histories that should not be collapsed into one origin story.【ref012】【ref022】

formation.text: Pictographic: the graph depicts an infant as a whole, rather than combining separately meaningful or phonetic parts. Early Shang forms are interpreted as emphasizing a large head, moving arms, and undeveloped or bundled legs; anatomical details are interpretations of the forms.【ref002】【ref012】【ref022】

history.text: The selected seal-script image is a modern redraw of a later reference form, distinct from the Shang forms discussed in paleographic accounts. It does not itself document the original pictograph or prove a sequence of graphic changes.【ref022】【ref023】【ref024】【ref025】

A historical account describes a more elaborate Shang graph, 𢀈, used for the first earthly branch, and says 子 gradually took its place after the beginning of Zhou. It also describes 子 as used for a child and for the sixth branch, later written 巳. A competing proposal identifies 甾 as the earlier first-branch graph; the sequence remains disputed.【ref004】【ref014】【ref022】

The Han-era lexicographic account associates 子 with the eleventh month and the growth of things. This is a later explanation of the graph, not evidence that “growth” was its original Shang meaning.【ref003】【ref005】【ref015】

The graph was also reportedly used loanwise for 慈 and 孜 in Western Zhou inscriptions: this is borrowing to write other words, not evidence that those words developed from the infant meaning. The source does not provide sound comparisons here, so the precise sound basis cannot be stated.【ref013】

uncertainties.text: The dossier supports an infant pictograph, but interpretations differ over its anatomical details. It does not establish an exact calendar date for the earliest child-use inscription; the Shang example and its reading are reported through a secondary account.【ref001】【ref002】【ref012】【ref013】【ref022】

The earlier graph for the first earthly branch and the timing or mechanism of changes in branch assignments are unresolved: accounts propose either 𢀈 or 甾 before 子. The available readings do not establish that the child and branch uses are connected by borrowing.【ref004】【ref014】【ref018】【ref019】【ref022】

Reported uses include a clan leader, a person suffix in Warring States Chu slips, and “young/immature.” The dossier does not establish a complete chronology connecting these uses to “infant,” or a semantic path to the additional glosses “offspring,” “seed,” and “fruit.”【ref006】【ref016】【ref022】

senses.period: Shang; exact earliest token date unresolved
senses.text: A paleographic account identifies “infant” as the graph’s original sense and reports a Shang pregnancy-related use in 有子. This is the earliest supported sense here, though the exact reading and calendar date are not independently established in the dossier.【ref012】【ref013】【ref022】

The graph is reported as used for a child in Shang contexts. This use fits the infant interpretation, but the evidence here does not establish a precise date or a separate semantic transition from “infant.”【ref012】【ref022】

子 is attested as the first earthly branch, but the identity of the graph used earlier and the reassignment sequence are disputed. One account places 𢀈 before 子; another proposal identifies 甾. The relationship to the infant sense is unresolved.【ref004】【ref014】【ref022】
A Shang use for a same-surname clan leader is reported. The evidence does not establish how this use developed from, or relates to, “infant.”【ref012】【ref022】
In 君子, 子 is reported as a suffix referring to a person. The dossier does not establish a complete semantic path from the child sense to this use.【ref016】【ref022】
A later use meaning “young” or “immature” is reported, as in 子薑. The evidence does not date or explain its development from the child sense.【ref016】
“Offspring” is a supplied dictionary gloss. The dossier does not independently document its chronology or establish its semantic connection to the earliest infant sense.【ref006】
“Seed” and “fruit” are supplied glosses; the dossier does not establish their history or a development from “infant” or “child.”【ref006】

developments.text: The reported child use is closely related in meaning to “infant,” but the dossier does not document a dated transition between them.【ref012】【ref022】

limitations.text: Reported uses do not establish a full chronology or semantic chain among infant, child, clan leader, person suffix, young, offspring, seed, and fruit. The branch use has a separately disputed graphic history.【ref004】【ref006】【ref014】【ref016】【ref022】

overview.text: 子 is a whole-graph picture interpreted as an infant. “Child” is an early supported use; its use for the first earthly branch has a separate, disputed history.【ref012】【ref022】【ref014】
